The early life stages of the Duck mussel are characterised by a parasitic glochidium larva that must attach to the gills of a suitable fish host to complete development. Upon excystment from the host, the newly metamorphosed juvenile measures just 0.0254 centimeters [Lb = 0.0254 centimeters] in shell length, a minute size that reflects the limited endogenous resources available during the non-feeding larval phase. This initial length is comparable to values reported for other unionid bivalves, although the reliance on host fish species introduces considerable variation in post-parasitic growth rates. In the laboratory, recently excysted juveniles were observed to initiate pedal feeding within hours of drop-off, transitioning rapidly from the lecithotrophic glochidium stage to an actively filtering post-metamorphic juvenile. The prodissoconch shell at this point is translucent and fragile, yet the animal is capable of burrowing into fine sediments within the first day. Such a small size at the onset of benthic life imposes high vulnerability to predation and physical disturbance, shaping the early demographic dynamics of wild populations.

As the juvenile bivalve grows, its shell elongates steadily through the first two years of benthic life. Field surveys of a Central European population indicate that individuals attain a shell length of approximately 3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 3 centimeters] at the onset of sexual maturation, which corresponds to an age of roughly two years based on modal analysis of size-frequency distributions. This length at puberty marks a key life-history transition, after which energy is partitioned between somatic growth and gamete production. Individuals smaller than this threshold are rarely found to be gravid in late spring, suggesting that a minimum body size is required before vitellogenesis can be initiated. The onset of gonad maturation is also influenced by local water temperature and food availability, with populations in warmer, more productive waters reaching this size earlier in the season. This value of 3 centimeters [Lp = 3 centimeters] is somewhat intermediate among European unionids, reflecting a moderate pace of pre-reproductive growth relative to congeneric species.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of laboratory culture at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], experimental assessments of reproductive output were conducted using gravid females collected from a lowland river system. The maximum daily reproductive rate was estimated by dividing the total number of glochidia released over a single spawning event by the duration of that release, yielding a value of approximately 41 glochidia per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 41 glochidia per spawning event], with females capable of producing multiple spawnings within a single reproductive season [F_R_i = multiple spawnings within a single reproductive season]. This rate, observed over a two-week period, is consistent with values reported for the closely related Unio tumidiformis at the same temperature, though the total fecundity per female can vary considerably with body size and nutritional condition. The controlled temperature of 17 °C was chosen to reflect typical late-spring water temperatures in the mussel's native range, when peak spawning activity is recorded. At this temperature, the release of glochidia is protracted rather than pulsed, a pattern that may increase the likelihood of encountering a compatible fish host.

Long-term mark-recapture studies in a Danish river system have provided robust estimates of the species' maximum lifespan. The oldest documented individual was recorded at 5,475 days [am = 5,475 days] at a mean annual water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a longevity that places Anodonta anatina among the longer-lived members of its genus. This estimate is based on a combination of shell annuli counts and repeated captures of individually marked mussels over a fifteen-year monitoring period. The value of 5,475 days corresponds to approximately fifteen years, which exceeds the typical lifespan reported for some faster-growing unionid species from warmer climates. Such extended longevity is often associated with a relatively low adult mortality rate and a reproductive strategy that spreads gamete production across many seasons. At this temperature regime of 17 °C, metabolic demands are moderate, which may contribute to the slow accumulation of senescent damage and the persistence of reproductively active adults well into their second decade.

Adult specimens of Anodonta anatina rarely exceed 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters] in ultimate total shell length, a value that represents the maximum size recorded across multiple European populations. This asymptotic size is typically attained only after 8 to 10 years of growth, after which the shell adds very little new material annually. The largest individuals are usually found in stable, nutrient-rich lake habitats where food particles are abundant year-round and predation pressure from fish and birds is relatively low. In contrast, populations inhabiting smaller, more hydrologically variable streams rarely produce mussels exceeding 10 centimeters in length, suggesting that resource limitation constrains the attainment of this ultimate size. The value of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters] is broadly consistent with the maximum sizes reported for other Anodonta species across the Palearctic, reinforcing the genus's reputation for achieving moderately large body sizes among freshwater bivalves. Senescent individuals approach this length asymptotically, with annual increments becoming negligible in the oldest age classes.
